figures.caption: Figure 1. EEG-Jev architecture and typed readouts. (a) A prefix with the system prompt, EEG embeddings, a natural-language question, an answer specification and a readout marker ⟨ R ⟩ form one input row. (b) A frozen REVE-L encoder processes multichannel EEG with electrode positions and time; a trainable connector maps its features to the language-model dimension. (c) The Qwen3.5-2B hybrid backbone has a frozen base and trainable LoRA adapters; u is the final normalized state at ⟨ R ⟩ . (d) Each question selects one readout. CHOICE matches a trainable projection of u against the candidates’ keys, ĉk =ck / rms ( ck ), where ck is the mean of their frozen text embeddings and d is the state dimension; NOUL gives the probability that a proposition holds, p ( yes ), shown as p(true); SCORE gives a distribution over task-specified numerical values v j and their probability-weighted expectation. The 0–10 bars and expected rating 5.42 illustrate a pain-rating example. Probabilities, scores, EEG traces and the scalp sketch are illustrative.

Figure 2. Question sampling and typed supervision. (a) Each training example pairs an EEG window with one of five question phrasings. For CHOICE the options are shuffled and the target index moves with the annotated option, here from slot 3 to slot 2. (b) Each training question is supervised through one type only: cross-entropy for CHOICE, binary cross-entropy for NOUL, and for SCORE a soft-target cross-entropy or a KL divergence, depending on the training stage, plus 0.2 times CRPS divided by the 10-point range. The SCORE target outline is a discrete Gaussian centred at 6.4; the prediction has mean 5.42. The batch-mean loss updates the connector, markers, LoRA and readouts; REVE-L and the backbone base stay frozen. Probabilities and EEG traces are illustrative, not model outputs.

Table 1. Data and evaluation scope. Each application uses one readout type; the core source of an application was fixed before the test evaluation and carries the main results. NB: sources that keep the windows, labels and subject splits of the NeuralBench code, release 0.4.0 (core task or full benchmark). Suppl.: supplementary sources with the same signal processing and our own windows, labels and subject splits; the nine pain sources are laser-pain studies from one research group and are not part of NeuralBench. Test: held-out subjects (patients for seizure) and windows, summed over sources; five motor-imagery sources split within subjects, and sources of one application can share participants. Per-source details: Table A1.

Table 2. Core-source test results from raw model outputs (post-processed: Table 3).NeuralBench best: externally reported, the highest mean test balanced accuracy (BA) among the models listed for the task in the NeuralBench results file (commit 7aaccf3, 10 October 2026, code release 0.4.0; mean ± s.d., three seeds)15,16. B1 is a per-source readout on frozen REVE-L features; B2 fine-tunes the last four REVE-L blocks per source. Both are trained in this study and scored on the same test windows as EEG-Jev (mean of seeds 7 and 8). BA in percent; MAE on the 0–10 scale. Seizure BA thresholds raw p ( yes ) at 0.5 and became the displayed metric after the evaluation; on the protocol’s primary metric, AUROC, EEG-Jev is below both baselines (0.825 vs 0.891 and 0.929; both paired intervals exclude zero). Bold: best value per row at the displayed precision among the three models of this study (EEG-Jev, B1, B2); NeuralBench best is not part of this comparison; ties bold together; bold does not indicate a significant difference. †: paired 95% interval of EEG-Jev minus this baseline excludes zero. All computed metrics: results/metrics-long.csv.

Table 3. Probability quality of EEG-Jev on the four core test sets, raw output → output after the frozen post-processing. The post-processing was fixed before the test evaluation: the prior correction uses class shares of the training draws and of the training set, and the temperature T was fitted on development data per application (motor imagery keeps T =1; SCORE has no class prior). NLL: negative log-likelihood; ECE: expected calibration error with ten equal-mass bins; CRPS/range: continuous ranked probability score divided by the range of the scale; coverage: percentage of ratings inside the central 80% predictive interval (nominal 80). BA in percent. Table 2 reports the raw outputs; this table shows what the post-processing changes. Both maps are monotone for the seizure probability, so AUROC is unchanged. The post-processing moves the seizure probability to the scale of the natural prevalence, so at a threshold of 0.5 sensitivity falls from 49.5% to 13.8% and BA with it; the threshold has to be set for the intended use.
